questions.question: Notice does not consist of
questions.answer:
**(C)** Salutation

A notice consists of the **name of the institution, the word NOTICE, the date, a heading or title, the body and the signature with the designation**. A **salutation** ("Dear Sir") is a part of a letter; nobody greets the readers of a notice. (*The solved booklet ticks "Title"; a title, however, is one of the essentials of a notice.*)

questions.question: In a formal letter, the name and address are written on the
questions.answer:
**(A)** Right margin

In the conventional Indian letter format the **sender's name and address are written at the top right corner** of the page, with the date below them, and the receiver's address begins at the left margin. The modern block form, which many schools now teach, lines everything at the left margin; the letter given in the answer to Q. 49 uses the block form.

questions.question: What is written at the beginning of an article?
questions.answer:
**(D)** Title

An article opens with a **title** (the writer's name usually follows it), and then the body in paragraphs. An address and a salutation belong to a letter; an article has no reader to be greeted.

questions.question: In report writing the narration of the event is always written in
questions.answer:
**(C)** the immediate past tense

A report records an event that has just taken place, so the narration is in the **past tense** — "the function began at 10 a.m.", "the Chief Guest planted a sapling". The report is written soon enough after the event for the details to be fresh, which is what "immediate" points at.

questions.question: Name the poem of the given lines: 'Fishermen in the cold sea / Would not harm whales / And the man gathering salt / Would look at his hurt hands.'
questions.answer:
**(C)** Keeping Quiet

These lines are from **Pablo Neruda's "Keeping Quiet"**. The poem imagines a moment of universal stillness in which the fisherman would not harm the whale and the salt-gatherer would stop to look at his **hurt hands** — the injuries of labour that ordinary busy life never lets him see.

questions.question: What does the poet expect the fishermen to do?
options: No to go in the sea
questions.answer:
**(A)** Not to harm whales

The extract says plainly, "Fishermen in the cold sea / **would not harm whales**" — in the poet's imagined silence the fisherman pauses and spares the whale. The poet does not tell the fisherman to give up the sea or to sit idle for ever. (*The solved booklet ticks "To be still"; the line of the extract is about not harming the whale.*)

questions.question: The man gathering salt would look at his
questions.answer:
**(B)** hurt hands

In "Keeping Quiet" the salt-gatherer, given a moment of stillness, "**would look at his hurt hands**" — hands cracked and burnt by the salt, which he has never had the time or the peace to notice. The image is the poem's sharpest picture of unregarded labour.

questions.question: 'They pace' is referred to
questions.answer:
**(C)** the tigers

"They pace" refers to the **tigers** embroidered by Aunt Jennifer: "They pace in sleek chivalric certainty" across the panel. Their confident pacing is set against the aunt's own trembling hands and the "massive weight of Uncle's wedding band".

questions.question: Franz looked for opportunities to skip school to do what?
questions.answer:
**(D)** Collect birds' eggs

Franz looked for a chance to skip school "**to look for birds' eggs**" or "to go sliding on the saar". It is the same boyish carelessness that makes him ashamed when he learns that it is the last French lesson he will ever have.

questions.question: Who describes interviews as being thumbprints on his windpipe?
questions.answer:
**(B)** Saul Bellow

The American novelist **Saul Bellow** called interviews "**thumbprints on my windpipe**" — a memorable protest against being pinned down and squeezed by questioners. Christopher Silvester quotes it as the classic statement of an author's dislike of the interview.

questions.question: Indigo is an excerpt from which book of the author?
questions.answer:
**(C)** *The Life of Mahatma Gandhi*

"Indigo" is an excerpt from **Louis Fischer's *The Life of Mahatma Gandhi*** (1950). Fischer had met Gandhi and had seen the Champaran campaign for himself; the chapter is his account of how the indigo sharecroppers' grievance became Gandhi's first civil-disobedience movement in India.

questions.question: Make-up room looked like a
questions.answer:
**(C)** hair-cutting salon

In "Poets and Pancakes" the make-up room of the Gemini Studios, with its mirrors, its bulbs and its crowd of actors being painted, "**looked like a hair-cutting salon**". (*The solved booklet ticks "Messy room"; the chapter's own image is the salon.*)

questions.question: What forces the children to live a life of exploitation?
questions.answer:
**(B)** Extreme poverty

Anees Jung's answer is **extreme poverty**. The ragpickers' children and the bangle makers of Firozabad are not exploited because their parents are wicked but because hunger leaves them no choice: "**food is more important for them than their identity**", and a child's wages are needed in the house. Poverty is the soil in which the traffic in child labour grows.

questions.question: What did William Douglas desire for?
questions.answer:
**(C)** To learn swimming

Douglas "**had a desire to learn to swim**" — it was that wish which took him to the YMCA pool at the age of ten or eleven, where he was thrown into the deep end and nearly drowned. (*The solved booklet ticks "Visit to California", which was his childhood trip to the beach, not his desire.*)

questions.question: What does the rattrap seller have to do to make his both ends meet?
questions.answer:
**(A)** Peddling

The rattrap seller lives by **peddling** — going from door to door with his rattraps and his "little business". The chapter says he had to keep body and soul together by begging and stealing as well, but his trade, the identity he is known by, is peddling.

questions.question: According to the poet, a thing of beauty is
questions.answer:
**(C)** a joy forever

Keats opens the poem with the line "**A thing of beauty is a joy for ever**": its loveliness "increases" and never passes into nothingness. Everything in the poem — the bower, the daffodils, the clear rills, the musk-rose — is offered as proof of that first statement.

questions.question: 'She soon put that thought out of her mind and
questions.answer:
**(A)** smiled

Seeing her mother's face "ashen like that of a corpse", the poet "**soon put that thought out of her mind**" and, at the airport, "**smiled and smiled and smiled**" — the same brave, deceptive smile that carries the poem's last line. (*She does look out of the car window at the young trees, but the line the question quotes ends in the smile.*)

questions.question: The tigers are not afraid of
questions.answer:
**(D)** the men beneath the tree

The poem says of the embroidered tigers, "**They do not fear the men beneath the tree**." The hunters are there, but the tigers are not afraid of them: it is Aunt Jennifer who is "ringed with ordeals" and afraid.

questions.question: What do the tigers do on the screen?
questions.answer:
**(D)** Prance

The poem's first lines are "Aunt Jennifer's tigers **prance** across a screen, / Bright topaz denizens of a world of green." "Prance" — stepping proudly — is the verb the poem gives them. (*The solved booklet ticks "Catch the prey", which the poem does not say.*)

questions.question: 'Pass into nothingness' means
questions.answer:
**(B)** never fade away

Keats says that "**it will never pass into nothingness**" — the beautiful thing will not die out or be lost. "Pass into nothingness" is to vanish; the poet says beauty will not. (*The solved booklet ticks "Never increase", which reverses the poem's "its loveliness increases".*)

questions.question: The poem 'Aunt Jennifer's Tigers' is by
questions.answer:
**(B)** Adrienne Rich

"Aunt Jennifer's Tigers" is by the American poet **Adrienne Rich**, who wrote it in 1951 while she was still a student. (*The solved booklet ticks Kamala Das; the poem is Rich's, and its theme of a woman's trapped life is characteristic of her early work.*)

questions.question: Maharaja and Dewan .................... the British officers to save the kingdom.
questions.answer:
**(B)** bribed

Kalki's narrator is blunt: the Maharaja "**bribed** the British officers" — with "**presents of diamond rings** and other things" — so that his kingdom might be saved and he might be left free to hunt his tigers. The satire is aimed at the whole machinery of princely collaboration.

questions.question: Who is the author of 'The Third Level'?
questions.answer:
**(D)** Jack Finney

"The Third Level" is by the American writer **Jack Finney**, a master of the "what if" story. It appeared in his collection *The Third Level* (1957) and is a favourite Class XII text for its quiet mixture of psychiatry and time travel.

questions.question: 'Why are we different from other Japanese?' Who said this?
questions.answer:
**(C)** Hana

**Hana** says this, in her own mind, as she and Sadao sit with the wounded American: "Why are we different from other Japanese?" It is the story's moral centre — the Sadaos are loyal Japanese who nevertheless cannot push a dying man back into the sea. (*The solved booklet ticks Sadao; the thought is Hana's.*)

questions.question: What were Derry and Mr. Lamb victim of?
questions.answer:
**(C)** Physical impairment

Derry's face was burnt by acid, and Mr. Lamb has **one leg** — a tin leg, lost in a bomb accident. Both are therefore **physically impaired**, and it is that shared fact which makes the old man the only person who can talk to the boy without pity.

questions.question: Zitkala was constantly observed by a woman who had
questions.answer:
**(A)** a pale face

Zitkala-Sa remembers being watched by "**a woman with a pale face**" — one of the palefaced staff of the Carlisle school, who followed the Indian girl and finally held her down while her long hair was cut. (*The solved booklet ticks "dark complexion"; the text's phrase is "paleface".*)

questions.question: 'We have to submit because they are strong.' These words were said by Judewin to
questions.answer:
**(A)** Zitkala-Sa

**Judewin**, who knew a little English, warned Zitkala-Sa: "**We have to submit because they are strong**" — the palefaces had decided to cut the boys' hair and would cut hers too. Zitkala-Sa refused to submit, hid under a bed and was dragged out; the scene is the heart of "The Cutting of My Long Hair".

questions.chapter: Journey to the End of the Earth
questions.question: Who was Geoff Green?
questions.answer:
**(B)** a Canadian

**Geoff Green** is a **Canadian**, the founder of the "**Students on Ice**" programme, which takes school and college students to the polar regions. Tishani Doshi travelled to Antarctica as part of his programme. (*The solved booklet ticks "A Britisher".*)

questions.question: What does 'hurt hand' refer to?
options: Growing insensitivity of man to pain
questions.answer:
**(D)** the growing insensitivity of man to pain

The salt-gatherer's "**hurt hands**" are the poem's image of **unnoticed suffering**. In the silence he would "look at his hurt hands" — that is, he would become aware of his own pain, and the rest of us of the pain our busyness ignores. The phrase indicts our **insensitivity to pain**, not the man's desires.

questions.question: What moves the 'pall from our lives'?
questions.answer:
**(D)** some shape of beauty

Keats writes that "**some shape of beauty moves away the pall / From our dark spirits**" — a lovely thing lifts the gloom that hangs over human life. (*The solved booklet ticks "strong bonds"; the poem's answer is beauty, which is its whole argument.*)

questions.question:
Read the passage on Rimpa Siva, the tabla player, and answer any six of the following:
(a) Who is Rimpa?
(b) At the age of five what surprised her father?
(c) Who heard her and what was her age at that time?
(d) Listening to the recording what did the Ustad think about Rimpa?
(e) How was Rimpa at the age of eleven at playing tabla?
(f) What has Rimpa changed by playing tabla?
(g) What was her biggest achievement?
(h) Write similar words from the passage: (i) conception (ii) wonder child.
questions.answer:
### (a)

**Answer.** Rimpa is **Rimpa Siva, a noted woman tabla player** — the daughter of **Pt. Swapan Siva**, himself "a noted tabla player" of a musical family.

**The passage's own words.**

> "Growing up in a musical family of Pt. Swapan Siva, a noted tabla player Rimpa heard the notes of the tabla all day in her house."

**Why she is important.** She was "hailed as a **child prodigy**", won "several awards including the **President's Award in 2007**", and had a documentary, *Rimpa Siva: Princess of Tabla*, made on her in France. Her story matters because it "**has changed the mindset**" about women tabla players.

### (b)

**Answer.** Her father was surprised to see her "**effortlessly mastering beats and rhythms**" which his **male students were still struggling at**.

**The passage's own words.**

> "When she was only five years old, her father saw her effortlessly mastering beats and rhythms which his male students were still struggling at."

**Why it surprised him.** A tabla needs years of practice, and the mastery of *bols* and *layas* is hard even for grown pupils. A five-year-old girl doing it without effort, in a tradition where the instrument was thought to belong to men, was the discovery of a prodigy.

### (c)

**Answer.** **Ustad Zakir Hussain** heard a **recording** of her, and she was **nine years old** at the time.

**The passage's own words.**

> "When Ustad Zakir Hussain heard a recording of a nine year old girl, he was deeply impressed."

**What followed.** He assumed "the player was at least 18 or 19 years old" — the recording sounded so mature. Two years later, on a visit to Kolkata, he **met the prodigy** and looked carefully at "the delicate fingers of an 11-year old girl".

### (d)

**Answer.** He was "**deeply impressed**" and thought that "the player was at least **18 or 19 years old**" — he could not believe that so confident and strong a performance had come from a child.

**The passage's own words.**

> "When Ustad Zakir Hussain heard a recording of a nine year old girl, he was deeply impressed. For he had thought that the player was at least 18 or 19 years old!"

**His later reaction.** When he met her in Kolkata, "he took a careful look at **Rimpa's fingers**, as though trying to understand how the delicate fingers of an eleven-year-old girl could produce such confident and strong notes.

### (e)

**Answer.** At eleven she was already a **child prodigy** whose playing was "**confident and strong**", so mature that the Ustad could not believe the player was a child.

**The passage's own words.**

> "He took a careful look at Rimpa's fingers, as though trying to understand how the delicate fingers of an 11-year old girl could produce such confident and strong notes."

**The point of the detail.** Her fingers were "delicate", her notes "strong": the contrast is exactly what the passage wants, because it overturns the assumption that a tabla is a man's instrument.

### (f)

**Answer.** She has changed "**the mindset**" — the general assumption that **tabla playing belongs to boys and men**.

**The passage's own words.**

> "When we think of Tabla players, images of boys or men come to our mind. The story of Rimpa Siva is one such story that has changed the mindset."

**How she changed it.** By mastering the instrument as a child prodigy, by winning "several awards including the President's Award in 2007", and by being the subject of a documentary — *Rimpa Siva: Princess of Tabla* — she made a woman tabla player a normal thing to see.

### (g)

**Answer.** The **President's Award in 2007**. That is the highest honour the passage names for her.

**The passage's own words.**

> "She won several awards including the President's Award in 2007. A documentary titled Rimpa Siva: 'Princess of Tabla' was made in France."

**The other achievement.** The documentary made on her in **France** — an honour that carried her name and her art to another country — is the second achievement the passage records, and it is the one that made her "Princess of Tabla".

### (h)

**Answer.** (a) Conception — **mindset**; (b) Wonder child — **prodigy** (child prodigy).

**As used in the passage.**

> "...The story of Rimpa Siva is one such story that has changed the **mindset**."

> "Early in her musical career, Rimpa had been hailed as a **child prodigy**."

**Note.** Both words are the passage's own. "Conception" is a way of thinking about something — here **mindset**; a "wonder child" is exactly a **prodigy**, a child of extraordinary talent.

questions.question: How did Douglas' experience at the beach in California affect him? (Answer in maximum 150 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Douglas was **three or four** when his father took him to a beach in California, and the experience left a mark that lasted for years.

**What happened.** "The waves were not so high... but they were **formidable**." One wave knocked him down and swept over him, and "**I was buried in water**"; when he came up "my breath was gone, I was frightened". He clung to his mother, but the sea's "**overpowering force**" had been felt.

**How it affected him.** He says the incident "**stirred the terror that was to come**" at the YMCA pool years later: it gave him a **lifelong aversion to water** which "stayed with him" and spoiled his fishing, canoeing and swimming, until he hired an instructor and conquered it in his thirties.

**The lesson he drew.** "**All we have to fear is fear itself**" — the fear was worse than the water.

questions.question: What are some positive views on interviews? (Answer in maximum 150 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Christopher Silvester records both sides, but the **defence** of the interview is put strongly.

**The positive views.** (i) In its **highest form** an interview is "**a source of truth**" — the shortest way of learning what a great mind actually thinks. (ii) It gives the public "**a vivid picture**" of the person behind the work, and in the age of the mass media it has become the **chief source of information**. (iii) It is a **democratic** form: it can be used to question power, not only to admire it.

**The examples in the chapter.** The extracts from interviews with **Umberto Eco** show an author thinking aloud, qualifying and revising as he speaks — something no finished essay can show. Eco himself treats the interview as a conversation that "produces something".

**The other side.** Against this stand the complaints of Kipling ("a crime"), Saul Bellow ("thumbprints on my windpipe") and the "phony" interviews of film stars.

questions.question: What will counting up to twelve and keeping still help us achieve? (Answer in maximum 150 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Counting to twelve and keeping still is Neruda's way of asking for a **moment of silence and self-examination** — a pause in the noise of the world.

**What it achieves.**
1. **A break in the hurry.** "Now we will count to twelve / and we will all keep still" — the counting measures out an interval in which nobody works, speaks or fights.
2. **Awareness of others' pain.** Given the pause, the fisherman "would not harm whales", the salt-gatherer "would look at his hurt hands", and the man who prepares "green wars" would "put on clean clothes and walk with his brothers".
3. **A gathering of the self.** The stillness would let us "**count to twelve**" and "**keep quiet**" — the poem's word for peace.

**The warning.** He does not want "**total inactivity**" or death: "**What I want should not be confused with total inactivity**." The silence is a pause in which life can begin again.

questions.question: How are Aunt Jennifer's tigers different from her? (Answer in maximum 150 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The tigers are everything Aunt Jennifer is not.

**The tigers.** They "**prance across a screen**", "bright topaz denizens of a world of green"; they are "**sleek and elegant**", they "pace in **chivalric certainty**" and "**do not fear the men beneath the tree**". They are fearless, free and sure of themselves, made of the Aunt's own needlework in colours that are bright and confident.

**Aunt Jennifer.** She sits "**with her needle**" and her fingers "**fluttering through her wool**"; she is timid, "**ringed with ordeals**", and she is mastered by "**Uncle's wedding band**", which sits "massively" on her hand.

**The contrast.** The tigers are the life she cannot live. Her art gives her creatures the freedom she lacks, and the poem's irony is that the confident tigers will go on prancing when she is dead, while "Aunt Jennifer's fingers" will still be "**terrified**".

questions.question: Who was Charley? What was his problem? (Answer in maximum 150 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Charley is the **narrator of "The Third Level"** — an ordinary New Yorker, married to Louisa, who works in an office and travels by the subway.

**His problem.** He had once taken the **subway and got off at a "third level"** of the Grand Central Station that does not exist, where the date was **1894**: old gas lamps, a man selling *The World*, dollars worth "a lot more", and a ticket to **Galesburg, Illinois**, his boyhood home. He wants to go back, and he keeps buying **old currency** — eight hundred dollars' worth — to be able to afford the fare.

**Why it is a problem.** His wife is anxious about this "**waking-dream wish to escape**", and his psychiatrist friend Sam calls it a "**hobby**" and then disappears into the same 1894 himself, sending Charley a first day cover from Galesburg.

questions.question: How did Derry's life change after meeting Mr. Lamb? (Answer in maximum 150 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Before the meeting Derry was a boy who **hated his own face** and expected everyone else to hate it. After it, he begins to think of himself as a person.

**What changed.**
1. **His idea of himself.** Mr. Lamb tells him "**it doesn't matter what they think**" and that he is "not the only one with a face like that"; Derry stops saying "I'm ugly" and starts saying "I'm going to be all right".
2. **His courage.** He goes back into the garden, and when his mother forbids it he **defies her** for the first time and returns to Mr. Lamb.
3. **His ambition.** He talks of what he will do with his life instead of only of what people think of him.

**The result.** When he comes back at the end and finds Mr. Lamb dead, he says he will stay — the promise is the measure of how far the old man's talking has brought him.

questions.question: How did Anan's advice to his sister Bama impact her? (Answer in maximum 150 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Anan's explanation — that the elder man carried the packet by its string because the **upper castes believed his touch would pollute** them — turned Bama's laughter into a **resolve that shaped her whole life**.

**What he told her.** That "**we too are human beings**"; that the humiliation was not natural but manufactured by caste; and that the way out was **education** — "if we studied and made progress, we could throw off these indignities".

**The impact.**
1. **Shame and anger.** She stopped laughing and felt "**a great sadness**" — the first political feeling of her life.
2. **Ambition.** She decided to study hard, "**to touch the books**" that the upper castes had kept to themselves.
3. **A writer's vocation.** The lesson became the story "We Too Are Human Beings", written so that other children would learn what she had learnt at eleven.

**In one line.** Anan gave her the words that turned a child's bewilderment into a lifetime's purpose.

questions.question: How is grandeur associated with 'Mighty Dead'? (Answer in maximum 150 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Keats speaks of "**the grandeur that we owe to the mighty dead**" — the beauty and dignity their lives leave behind for us. The line comes in the list of "**lovely tales**" that bind us to the earth:

> "And such too is the grandeur of the dooms / We have imagined for the mighty dead; / All lovely tales that we have heard or read."

**What it means.** The **"dooms"** — the deaths and destinies we imagine for the great of the past — are themselves a **source of beauty**: the heroes of story and history, and the tales told about them, are a "shape of beauty" that lifts the "pall" from our spirits.

**Why it fits the poem.** Keats is arguing that beauty comes from many sources — nature, art, music and **the memory of the great dead** — and that all of them are "a joy for ever" and keep us alive.

questions.question: You are Sunil/Swati, the Secretary of Gandhi Public School, Ranchi. Write a suitable notice for your school notice board requesting names of the students for participation in a cultural programme to be organised by your school. (Answer in maximum 250 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**GANDHI PUBLIC SCHOOL, RANCHI**

**NOTICE**

*18 October 2026*

**CULTURAL PROGRAMME — NAMES INVITED**

A **cultural programme** will be held in the school auditorium on **Saturday, 14 November 2026, at 4 p.m.** on the occasion of the school's annual day. Students who wish to take part should give their names to the undersigned **through their class teachers by 25 October 2026**.

**Items.** (1) Group dance — folk and classical; (2) solo and group song in Hindi, English or a regional language; (3) one-act play and skit; (4) elocution on "My School, My Pride"; (5) poetry recitation; (6) instrumental music; (7) a short mime.

**Conditions.** A student may offer a maximum of two items. **Auditions** will be held on **28 and 29 October at 2 p.m. in the auditorium**; music tracks must be brought on a pen drive at the time of the audition; costumes and props are the participants' responsibility. Selected students must attend rehearsals on **10 and 12 November**.

The final list will be put up on the notice board on **1 November**.

**Swati**
Secretary, Cultural Committee

**Format points.** Institution at the top, the word NOTICE, date, heading, **what, when, where, the entry deadline, the auditions and the conditions**, and the signature with the office held.

questions.question: You are Priya/Pankaj, a student of Class 12. You lost your notebook during the lunch-break. You want it back. Write a notice for the school notice board giving its details. (Answer in maximum 250 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**S. N. +2 HIGH SCHOOL, RANCHI**

**NOTICE**

*4 August 2026*

**LOST: A NOTEBOOK**

I lost my **notebook** somewhere in the school campus during the **lunch-break today, 4 August**, between 12.30 and 1 p.m.

**Description.** It is a **thick, brown-covered register of about 200 pages**, with a rubber band round it and my name, **Priya, Class XII-B**, written in blue ink on the front cover. The last page carries a red-ink remark by the chemistry teacher, and a page near the middle has a pressed neem leaf in it. The notebook is **not a printed one** — it is handwritten and contains my notes on all five subjects.

**How important it is.** The notes cannot be replaced, as they cover the whole year's work and the half-yearly examination is next week.

Anyone who finds it is requested to hand it over to me in **Class XII-B** during the break, or to leave it with the **school office**, and to inform me at once. I shall be grateful for the kindness.

**Priya**
Class XII-B

**Format points.** Institution, NOTICE, date, heading, **what was lost, when and where, identifying marks, why it matters and what to do**, with the signature and the class.

questions.question: You are Mita/Manoj. Write a letter to the Editor complaining about the drainage system creating problems for the people of your locality. (Answer in maximum 250 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**Mita**
**14, Harmu Road**
**Ranchi**
**6 July 2026**

The Editor
*The Daily Pioneer*
Ranchi

**Subject: Broken drainage system of Harmu Road and the suffering of the residents**

Sir

Through the columns of your esteemed daily I wish to draw the attention of the Municipal Commissioner to the **drainage system of Harmu Road**, which has broken down completely.

**The condition of the drains.** The drains on both sides of the road have not been cleaned for over a year. Their concrete covers have broken at three places, and the mouth of the main drain near the bus stop is blocked with polythene and silt, so that the water stands there for weeks. The side drains have cracked, and the sewage now seeps into the lanes behind the market.

**The problems it creates.** Every rain floods the road knee-deep, and the water enters the shops and the ground-floor houses. The standing water breeds mosquitoes, and more than twenty families on the road have had fever this month. Children walk to school through this water, and the stench makes the area unbearable in the evening. A stray dog fell into the open drain last week.

**The remedy.** I request the department to **desilt and repair the drains before the rest of the monsoon**, to replace the broken covers, to close the open mouth of the main drain with a grating, and to arrange a monthly cleaning schedule. A little expenditure now will prevent an epidemic later.

Yours faithfully
**Mita**

**Format points.** Sender's address and date, addressee, subject, the **complaint with concrete details and consequences**, a set of remedies, and the formal close.

questions.question: A tree plantation day was organised in your locality. Write a report giving details of the programme. You are Seema/Sanjay from 'The Express'. (Answer in maximum 250 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**FIVE HUNDRED SAPLINGS PLANTED ON TREE PLANTATION DAY**

*By Sanjay, Staff Correspondent*

**Ranchi, 12 July 2026.** A **tree plantation day** was organised by the Harmu Road Residents' Welfare Society on Sunday, 12 July, in the lane behind the community hall and along the bank of the nullah, from 7 a.m. to 11 a.m.

**The programme.** The day began with a short ceremony at the community hall, where the **Ward Councillor, Mrs. Kamla Devi**, planted a **peepal sapling** and spoke about the falling water table of Ranchi and the need for shade in a growing city. The **forest department** had supplied five hundred saplings — neem, peepal, gulmohar, jamun and amaltas — along with tree guards for two hundred.

**Who took part.** Nearly **one hundred and fifty residents**, including schoolchildren and college students on their holidays, planted the saplings in rows along the nullah and in the parks at both ends of the lane. Members of the society's youth wing dug the pits, and the biscuit factory nearby supplied drinking water and lunch.

**The pledge.** The society decided that each family would **water and guard two saplings** for a year, and a register was kept of the names. The Councillor promised a second plantation in August, before the rains end.

**Format points.** Headline, byline, place and date, the **sequence of the programme, the numbers, the names and the closing resolve**, all in the past tense, with no personal opinion.

questions.question: Write an article on 'Need to Save Water'. (Answer in maximum 250 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**EVERY DROP COUNTS: THE NEED TO SAVE WATER**

Water is the one thing we cannot manufacture. Three-fourths of the earth is covered with it, but only a fraction of one per cent is fresh and available to us — and that fraction is shrinking.

**The danger.** Our cities are already drawing water from more than a hundred feet below the ground, and the water table in Ranchi and Patna has fallen by several metres in ten years. The rivers carry sewage and industrial waste; the tubewells in many villages yield iron or fluoride. Summer arrives early now, and the water tanker has become a familiar sight in the lanes of our towns. In a country whose farmers depend on the monsoon, a dry spell is a threat to the harvest and to every meal on the table.

**What can be done.** Close every tap. Repair every leak — a dripping tap wastes forty litres a day. Take a bucket instead of a shower; wash the car with a bucket, not a pipe. Harvest the rain from the roof into a pit or a tank; in towns, recharge the ground with rainwater instead of letting it run into the drain. Grow trees, which hold the soil and the moisture; and farm with drip irrigation instead of flooding the field.

**The habit.** Water saved is water that grows food, that fills a school tap, and that quenches a village with a dry well.

**Format points.** A title, an opening statement of the problem, a paragraph on the **causes and consequences**, a paragraph of remedies, and a short firm conclusion — within 250 words.

questions.question: Write an article on 'Social Media and its Impact'. (Answer in maximum 250 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**SOCIAL MEDIA: A TOOL IN OUR HANDS**

The town market of fifty years ago stood at the crossroads of the village. Today it has moved into the phone in every pocket: a place where a thousand opinions are shouted, a thousand pictures are shown, and every young person meets the whole world at once.

**The gains.** Social media has given the unheard a voice. A student in a small town can attend a lecture given in another continent; a farmer can check the price of his crop before he sells it; a lost child is found in hours through a forwarded photograph; and business, from a tailoring shop to a coaching centre, runs on the phone. For a generation of learners, this is a library that never shuts.

**The harm.** The same screen takes away what study needs — time, silence and attention. A student with a phone beside his book reads the same page three times. It breeds comparison and envy, and young people measure their worth by the number of likes on a photograph. Worse, it spreads rumour faster than truth: an unverified message can start a riot, and a photograph can destroy a reputation in an evening.

**What must be done.** Not abstinence, which rarely works, but discipline: a time limit, no phone during study hours and none in the bedroom at night, and a habit of checking a claim before forwarding it. The tool is neutral; the hand that holds it decides.

**Format points.** A title, the **gains and the harms in balance**, a paragraph on remedies, and a firm conclusion — within 250 words.
